prompt:
Use case: scientific-educational. Asset: production sprite atlas for Cosmic: A Sea Beneath the Moon. Input image1 is a STYLE reference only: retain the medallion form, palette, grain and physical depiction approach, but create the NEW requested subjects below. Exactly 4 columns by 4 rows, 16 circles total. Regular equal square cells, landscape4:3 ratio for12circles or square for16circles. Aim2048px wide. Every circle diameter84%of its cell, centred, with generous fully transparent gutters; leave allcells complete and separated. No extra cells or objects. Original astronomical chromolithograph with dry-gouache and chalk masses: deep indigo circular fields, feathered warm-ivory light, amber heat, copper/charcoal minerals and restrained teal water. Simplify to broad meaningful structures visible at72px. Fine grain stays in subjects; generous quiet dark space. One thin ivory circular outline. No glossy UI buttons, photographic lens flare, ornamental decoration, humans, machines, text, labels, numerals, formulas or grid lines. Inside each circle the field is opaque; outside circles true alpha transparency. No shadows, rays or fragments beyond circles. Atom/particle diagrams are schematic: tiny compact ivory dots and diffuse electron-probability clouds, never planetary electron orbits; individual nuclei do NOT glow like stars. Exact invisible chemistry is communicated by game names/readings, never by invented diagnostic coloration. All terrestrial worlds have bare mineral terrain; no plants, life or modern continents. Early Moon is pale gray-ivory without familiar dark maria. All Earth cutaways are views of one continuing world.
Strict row-major subjects (left to right, then top to bottom):
1. A helium-rich stellar core: Cutaway of the established massive star with one broad smooth central core and a thin surrounding hot shell. Avoid: A core-region view; colour does not identify helium and the label carries composition.
2. A helium-burning core: The same core cutaway with a bright active central region and outward feathered heat texture. Avoid: Activity rather than invented elemental colour; nuclear-burning identity needs context.
3. Carbon-rich stellar material: A close view of hot stellar core material inside a curved shell edge, a few schematic merging nuclear clusters. Avoid: Not soot or charcoal; carbon abundance is label-dependent, nuclear diagram not literal surface detail.
4. Oxygen-rich stellar material: The same hot core-material convention with a curved shell edge and a sparse cluster capturing a small nuclear group. Avoid: No blue oxygen gas or bubbles; schematic nuclear process, composition needs its label.
5. Carbon-burning layers: A partial stellar cutaway with a bright inner burning band around a denser centre. Avoid: Shell position is schematic; no claim that material colour reveals carbon.
6. Oxygen-burning layers: A deeper cutaway detail with a narrow luminous burning band nested inside two broader surrounding layers. Avoid: Use depth and active band placement; exact burning fuel requires label.
7. An onion of burning shells: A single star with a generous wedge removed, showing four broad nested burning shells and a small centre. Avoid: One star, no separate floating spheres; broad bands survive reduction.
8. Silicon-burning material: A close stellar cutaway with a very compact bright inner reaction region surrounded by thick nested shells. Avoid: Hot active nuclear region; never silicon crystals or sand.
9. An iron-group core: The same layered star with a small dense unlit central core enclosed by luminous surrounding shells. Avoid: No exposed metallic ball; dense inert centre is conceptual, composition label-dependent.
10. Gravity without fusion support: A layered stellar outline enclosing a centre with strong short inward cues and compressed central material. Avoid: Force/process view; no black-hole disk and no outward explosion.
11. A flood of neutrinos: Many very fine nearly straight dotted trajectories streaming through and out of a small dense core. Avoid: Diagrammatic invisible-particle paths; no laser beams, jets or visible neutrino colour.
12. A collapsing stellar core: A tiny dense centre with a broad converging mantle and tightly inward swept strokes. Avoid: Still collapsing, with infall; a finished remnant has a clear stable edge.
13. An outward supernova shock: A bright incomplete outward-moving circular shock front within the dark stellar envelope. Avoid: One leading front inside the star, not detached debris or a giant's pulsating surface.
14. Pressure in dense neutron-rich matter: A close packed dense cluster confined inside a tiny core, with short outward cues opposed by inward ones. Avoid: Conceptual pressure balance in matter, not mechanical springs or a shield.
15. A neutron star: A very small sharp ivory remnant surrounded by a large dark field, with no accretion disk or mandatory jets. Avoid: Relative compactness is contextual; no claim that isolated pictures prove stellar density.
16. A hot stellar remnant: The same tiny neutron-star disk with a soft fading thermal halo, otherwise empty space. Avoid: Stored heat shown by halo; do not invent pulsar beams or a second object.
